questions.prompt: A stopwatch consistently reads 0.2 s too high because of a fault. This is an example of:
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — a consistent offset in every reading is a systematic error.
questions.feedbackWrong: Systematic errors shift every reading the same way — consistency is the tell. Random errors scatter readings about the true value.

mistakes.misconception: Treats all measurement error as random.
mistakes.correction: Random errors vary reading-to-reading; a CONSTANT offset is systematic and cannot be reduced by repeating and averaging.

questions.prompt: A length is measured as 45.0 cm ± 0.5 cm and a width as 20.0 cm ± 0.5 cm. Calculate the area and explain how to combine the uncertainties.

markScheme.text: When multiplying, PERCENTAGE uncertainties add: 0.5/45 ≈ 1.1% and 0.5/20 = 2.5% give ≈ 3.6%.
Absolute uncertainty ≈ 3.6% of 900 ≈ ±32 cm² — report as 900 ± 32 cm².

mistakes.misconception: Adds absolute uncertainties (±1 cm²) when multiplying quantities.
mistakes.correction: Absolute uncertainties add only for addition/subtraction. Multiplication and division add PERCENTAGE uncertainties.

questions.prompt: A current of 2.5 A is measured with an uncertainty of ±0.1 A. Calculate the percentage uncertainty, in percent.
When plotting a graph to test the relationship y = mx + c, the gradient of the straight line gives:
options: The value of x at y = 0
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — gradient is m; the y-intercept is c.
questions.feedbackWrong: In y = mx + c form, the gradient of the line IS m, and the y-intercept is c.

mistakes.correction: Gradient measures the rate (m); the intercept is where the line crosses the y-axis (c).

questions.prompt: Describe an experiment to measure the Young modulus of a wire: the measurements you would take, the graph you would plot, and how the Young modulus is obtained.
questions.guidance: Think about what stress and strain each require.

markScheme.text: Measure the wire's diameter with a micrometer (several positions, averaged) for cross-sectional area, and the original length.
Add known masses/forces and measure the extension each time — repeat and average.
Plot stress (force/area) against strain (extension/original length) — or force vs extension as an alternative valid approach.
Young modulus = gradient of the linear stress-strain region (or gradient × length/area for the force-extension version).

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between repeatability, reproducibility and resolution in experimental measurements.

markScheme.text: Repeatability: same method, same observer, same equipment — how close repeated readings are.
Reproducibility: DIFFERENT observers/equipment still obtain close results.
Resolution: the smallest change in the quantity the instrument can detect — set by the scale or digit step.

questions.prompt: A wire of length 2.0 m and cross-sectional area 0.50 mm² has resistance 0.072 Ω. Calculate the resistivity in units of 10⁻⁸ Ω·m (enter the mantissa, e.g. 1.8 for 1.8×10⁻⁸).
A calculated value is 3.2471 V and the uncertainty is ±0.1 V. How should the result be reported?
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — the value should be quoted to the same precision as the uncertainty.
questions.feedbackWrong: Report the value to the same decimal precision as the uncertainty: ±0.1 V means one decimal place, so 3.2 ± 0.1 V.

mistakes.correction: Extra digits are false precision — they claim certainty the measurement doesn't have.
